title: C-reactive protein
subtitle: Inflammatory marker interpreted with timing and clinical context
summary: Inflammatory marker interpreted with timing and clinical context
introduction: CRP is a non-specific marker of inflammation. It begins rising several hours after an inflammatory stimulus and may peak around 48 hours, so an early normal result does not exclude serious infection or inflammation.

rows.name: Within laboratory range
lowInterpretation: Makes a substantial systemic inflammatory response less likely at that moment.

rows.name: Mild elevation
highInterpretation: Can occur with mild inflammation, early infection, viral illness, tissue injury, obesity or chronic inflammatory disease.

rows.name: Moderate elevation
highInterpretation: Supports clinically important inflammation or infection but is not diagnostic of bacterial infection.

rows.name: Marked elevation
highInterpretation: Raises concern for substantial bacterial infection, major inflammation, tissue injury or other serious pathology; interpret with the patient rather than the number alone.

rows.name: Rising CRP
rows.referenceRange: Compare serial results and time interval
highInterpretation: May indicate evolving inflammation, inadequate source control or expected delayed peak. A rising result is not automatically treatment failure without clinical context.

rows.name: Falling CRP
rows.referenceRange: Compare serial results and clinical state
highInterpretation: A falling CRP does not override deterioration, new hypoxia, hypotension, confusion or another new clinical concern.

urgentFindings: Do not use a low CRP to discharge a patient with hypotension, new confusion, hypoxia, rigors, mottled skin, reduced urine output or rapidly progressive symptoms.
A normal or mildly raised CRP early in illness does not exclude sepsis, pneumonia, pyelonephritis, appendicitis or another serious infection.
A CRP >100 mg/L is not itself a diagnosis or an automatic indication for antibiotics; identify the source and assess physiology.
Immunosuppressed patients may have a reduced inflammatory response despite serious infection.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Early normal/mild CRP with a sick-looking patient
findings: CRP normal or only mildly raised
Recent onset of symptoms (typically within a few hours)
Physiological derangement or high-risk features on examination
interpretation: CRP rises over hours and can peak around 48 hours, so an early result does not exclude serious infection, sepsis or another acute inflammatory process
Physiology and clinical assessment take priority over a reassuring-looking CRP this early
actions: Do not use a low or mildly raised early CRP to downgrade concern in a physiologically unwell patient (see urgent findings)
Treat and escalate on clinical findings and observations; consider repeating CRP later in the illness if the diagnosis remains unclear
Request FBC and consider blood cultures/further source-specific testing if sepsis is suspected (see further testing)

commonPatterns.title: Blunted CRP response in immunosuppression
findings: CRP normal or lower than expected for the apparent severity of illness
Immunosuppression: chemotherapy, high-dose steroids, biologic therapy, transplant recipient or known immunodeficiency
interpretation: Immunosuppressed patients can mount a reduced inflammatory response despite serious or life-threatening infection, so a normal CRP is far less reassuring in this group
actions: Treat neutropenic sepsis or other suspected serious infection as time-critical regardless of a normal CRP (see urgent findings)
Request FBC to check neutrophil count alongside CRP (see further testing)
Have a lower threshold for escalation and senior/medical review in immunosuppressed patients

commonPatterns.title: Markedly raised CRP — source identification needed
interpretation: Raises concern for substantial bacterial infection, major inflammation or tissue injury, but is not itself a diagnosis and does not automatically mean antibiotics are required
The priority is identifying the source and assessing physiology, not treating the number in isolation
actions: Actively look for a source: examine systematically and consider urinalysis, chest assessment, abdominal examination and wound/line sites
Assess physiology (observations, mental state, urine output) and escalate per local sepsis pathway if criteria are met
Request further targeted testing based on the suspected source (see further testing)

commonPatterns.title: Rising CRP despite treatment
findings: CRP higher than a previous result
Patient already receiving treatment (e.g. antibiotics) for a presumed infective/inflammatory source
interpretation: Can reflect an expected delayed peak rather than treatment failure, but can also indicate inadequate source control, a resistant organism, or a wrong or missed diagnosis
The clinical trajectory matters as much as the CRP trend — a rising CRP in an improving patient is different from a rising CRP in a deteriorating one
actions: Reassess the patient clinically rather than reacting to the CRP number alone — check observations, symptoms and examination for improvement or deterioration
Consider whether the source has been adequately identified and controlled (e.g. drainage, line removal, correct antibiotic choice)
Arrange medical review if the patient is deteriorating or the CRP continues to rise beyond the expected timeframe

commonPatterns.title: Falling CRP with a new clinical concern
findings: CRP lower than a previous result
New hypoxia, hypotension, confusion, mottled skin or another new deterioration
interpretation: A falling CRP generally supports improvement but does not override a new, independent sign of deterioration — CRP lags clinical status and does not fall instantly even with effective treatment
actions: Do not use a falling CRP to reassure against a new, independently concerning clinical sign (see urgent findings)
Reassess the patient directly and escalate based on current physiology and symptoms, not the CRP trend alone

rationale: White cell count and neutrophil differential add complementary information to CRP, particularly in immunosuppressed patients where CRP may be a less reliable marker
Identifies a causative organism and guides antibiotic choice when a significant bacterial infection or sepsis is suspected
Quick, immediately available test to help identify a urinary source contributing to a raised CRP
Assesses renal function and hydration status, which inform severity assessment and treatment (e.g. antibiotic dosing, fluid resuscitation) alongside a raised CRP
Lactate helps identify hypoperfusion or sepsis severity when CRP is markedly raised or the patient looks unwell
A single value can be misleading given the delayed rise and peak; the trend over serial results, alongside clinical trajectory, is more useful than one isolated value
